1. Introduction
We consider the distributional version of Learning from Expert Advice (LEA), which is a two-player
repeated game between a learning algorithm and an adversary. Let d ∈ N+ be the total number of
experts. In each (t-th) round, the two players interact as follows.

1. The learning algorithm picks a distribution pt ∈ ∆(d) over the d experts, where ∆(d) ⊂ Rd
   denotes the probability simplex, i.e., ∆(d) = {p ∈ Rd : p ≥ 0, ∥p∥1 = 1}.
2. The adversary observes pt and picks a vector lt ∈ [−1, 1]d specifying the losses of all experts.
3. The algorithm observes lt and suffers a loss defined by the inner product ⟨pt , lt ⟩.
4. The adversary determines whether the game terminates. If so, let T be the total number of rounds.

Techniques Our algorithm is based on the following idea. It is already known that ϕ-regret
minimization in LEA can be reduced to an external regret minimization problem on the stochastic
matrix space S(d) (Gordon et al., 2008), for which solutions can be built as variants of mirror
descent. Deviating from the latter part of this standard procedure, we apply a linear transform on the
unconstrained matrix space Rd×d , converting all the comparing ϕ’s to their corresponding transform
domain coefficients. If ϕ is sparse on the transform domain, then we see it as “simple” – just like the
intuition from Fourier transform, where time series consisting of very few frequencies are considered
simple. Then, since learning a hypothesis ϕ is equivalent to learning its transform domain coefficient,
we can apply a sparsity-adaptive online learning algorithm to perform this task, for which there are
out-of-the-box options available (Orabona, 2025, Chapter 10).

1.1. Related Work
Φ-regret The ϕ-regret we study is an instance-dependent version of a better-known concept called
the Φ-regret, due to Greenwald and Jafari (2003). With respect to any class Φ ⊂ S(d) of action
modification rules, the Φ-regret is defined as the supremum of RegretT (ϕ) over all ϕ ∈ Φ. Due to
its generality unifying external, internal and swap regret, further developments have been presented
in numerous works afterwards, particularly regarding its connection to various equilibrium concepts
in game theory (Stoltz and Lugosi, 2007; Rakhlin et al., 2011; Piliouras et al., 2022; Bernasconi
et al., 2023; Cai et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024a).
     Technically, we build on the well-known reduction from swap regret to external regret on the
extended domain S(d), pioneered by Stoltz and Lugosi (2005); Blum and Mansour (2007); Gordon
et al. (2008) and further developed by Ito (2020). In a conceptually different manner, one may also
analyze the swap regret through the subsequence regret (Lehrer, 2003; Roth, 2023), and unifying
algorithms have been proposed based on certain multi-objective formulations of online learning
(Lee et al., 2022; Haghtalab et al., 2023; Noarov et al., 2023) related to the L∞ -norm Blackwell
approachability of the negative orthant (Blackwell, 1956; Perchet, 2015; Shimkin, 2016). The key
idea here is to convert the subsequence regret to the regret of a “meta” LEA algorithm that reweighs
different subsequences. In particular, utilizing the meta algorithm of Chen√et al. (2021), the approach
of Roth (2023) can achieve an instance-dependent refinement of the Õ( T ) internal regret bound
(see Appendix D). Generic reductions between Blackwell approachability and no-regret learning
have also been studied by Abernethy et al. (2011); Dann et al. (2023, 2024).
     A recent breakthrough of Dagan et p  al. (2024) and Peng and Rubinstein (2024) showed that the
d-dependence of the time-averaged Õ( d/T ) swap regret bound can be improved exponentially,
at the price of an exponentially worse dependence on T . This is orthogonal to the regime of
T ≫ d we consider, but very intriguingly, their algorithms are √    also based on some sort of multi-
resolution analysis. Closer to our setting, they showed that the Õ( dT ) swap regret is optimal in the
distributional version of LEA with T ≫ d, answering an open problem from earlier works.

Adaptive online learning This work aligns with the general theme of adaptivity in online learning,
e.g., (McMahan and Orabona, 2014; Foster et al., 2015; Cutkosky, 2018; Mhammedi and Koolen,
2020), whose main idea is to achieve regret bounds that scale with a priori unknown complexity
measures of the problem instance. Existing approaches can be roughly categorized into two types:
the first type uses a generic expert meta algorithm to aggregate multiple copies of a “non-adaptive”
base algorithm (e.g., mirror descent with fixed learning rate) with different hyperparameter setups
(Foster et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2021), while the second type uses specialized designs to eschew
the expert aggregation (Duchi et al., 2011; Luo and Schapire, 2015; Zhang et al., 2024b; Cutkosky
and Mhammedi, 2024), trading generality for computational efficiency. Our approach belongs to the
second type.

2. Technical Ingredients
The starting point of our approach is the celebrated ϕ-to-external reduction of Gordon et al. (2008).
This is remarkably simple, with similar ideas also presented in several works around the same time
(Stoltz and Lugosi, 2005; Blum and Mansour, 2007). First, let us assume access to a computational
oracle which, given any input ϕ ∈ S(d), returns a fixed point p ∈ ∆(d) satisfying p = ϕ(p). The
existence of p is due to Brouwer’s fixed-point theorem, and in practice, it can be obtained using
O(d3 ) time and O(d2 ) memory via a generic linear system solver.3

4. Conclusion
Focusing on the LEA problem with T ≫ d, this paper leverages the ideas of features and sparsity
to refine the classical reduction approaches in ϕ-regret and swap regret minimization (Blum and
Mansour, 2007; Gordon et al., 2008). We present an LEA algorithm with an adaptive ϕ-regret upper
bound, matching the external, internal and swap regret of specialized algorithms while improving
them in the intermediate regimes. Conceptually, our key observation is that incorporating certain
Haar-wavelet-inspired matrix features can introduce inductive biases that are well-aligned with
important special cases of the ϕ-regret. Technically, we show that the Haar wavelet is naturally
congruent
   √       with the benign gradient structure from the ϕ-to-external reduction, such that the optimal
Õ( dT ) swap regret bound can still be achieved after incorporating such matrix features. We leave
a thorough study of the downstream benefits to future works. In addition, the readers are referred
to (Hait et al., 2025) for technical improvements on this topic, as well as a concrete application to
learning in games.
